blindSummary:
This is a relatively safe destination for transgender visitors. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021 — a genuine turning point — and LGBTIQ organisations can now register and operate legally (a national pride group and an LGBTIQ umbrella organisation). The government engages with a UN equality campaign at the level of the courts and the cabinet.

Trans women report violence and discrimination remain widespread (trans people 4x more likely to experience assault), and there is no legal gender recognition, but there is no criminalisation, no police targeting pattern, and a monarchy-led culture that discourages open aggression. Tourism is tightly regulated (a per-day visitor levy), which incidentally provides visitors a structured, monitored environment.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): this country decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021; LGBTIQ organisations can register (though the process is lengthy). No stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit SOGISC protections; legal gender recognition is unavailable in practice, though authorities previously allowed some changes.

National broadcaster (Nov 2024): report that trans women face hurdles in reporting violence - trans people are over four times more likely to experience assault; a 49-year-old trans woman describes having nowhere to report assaults, family pressure to accept violence as fate, and laws that serve only men and women.

UN agency report with a title about fostering awareness and advancing LGBT+ inclusivity (March 2025, 37pp): the 2024 UN equality campaign advanced LGBTIQ+ equality among policymakers, parliamentarians and institutions (senior courts, the attorney general's office, the cabinet secretariat), securing the first direct dialogue between the LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians in the country's history.

Decriminalisation news site (June 2019): the lower house voted nearly unanimously (43-1) to repeal the 'unnatural sex' provisions (punishable by 1 month to 1 year, unenforced for at least 15 years); the director of a leading LGBTIQ organisation called the vote a first journey towards equality.

Decriminalisation news site (March 2021): the country's penal-code amendment act came into force on 17 Feb 2021 - after the upper house reinserted the provision, a joint sitting clarified that homosexuality between adults would not be considered unnatural sex; decriminalisation completed.

National broadcaster feature on the colours of the rainbow: the emergence of the country's LGBT community via its first LGBT Facebook page; profiles of the page's administrators and one of only two trans women living publicly (who fought to wear the traditional national dress to school at 16); notes self-stigma is significant but discrimination is described as not very widespread.

International magazine (Oct 2015): the country's small LGBT population has experienced very little persecution or violence, but the concept of being gay or trans is described as pretty much unheard of; there is no shared language for these identities; lesbianism is under-recognised; an activist created the first public LGBT outlet (the Facebook page) in 2013.
blindLocalsOnly: No legal gender recognition — resident-facing; the 4x assault likelihood and violence/discrimination reports describe residents' experience.
blindTangential: The 2021 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
